definition: The number of requests, tokens, or predictions a system can process per unit of time.
details: Throughput and latency often trade off against each other; systems can be tuned (e.g., via batching) to prioritize one over the other depending on the application's requirements.

explainer.lead: Throughput is the number of requests, tokens, or predictions a system processes per unit of time. It matters because it determines how much work a deployed system can handle.

tiers.eli5: It is how many things a system can get done in a minute—like counting how many customers a shop can serve per hour.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers raise throughput with techniques such as batching, then measure it against latency targets. A pitfall is that throughput and latency often trade off, so tuning for one can degrade the other.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined as requests, tokens, or predictions processed per unit of time. Its known limit is the trade-off with latency: systems can be tuned, e.g. via batching, to prioritize one over the other depending on application requirements.

explainer.example: A serving stack that batches many requests together can process more tokens per second, but each individual request may then wait longer for its response.
